title: The Last Good King
sum: 1 Esdras opens at the high point of Judah's last century: Josiah's Passover in Jerusalem in his eighteenth year (about 622 BC). Priests in their robes, Levites set free from carrying the ark, thousands of lambs and calves from the king and his officers, singers and gatekeepers at their posts: no Passover like it since Samuel. Then two sentences found in no Hebrew book praise Josiah's upright heart and say the judgment on Israel's sins already stood (1:21–22).

The rest of the chapter runs downhill. Pharaoh marches to the Euphrates; Josiah blocks him at Megiddo, ignoring "the words of Jeremiah the prophet," and dies. Three sons and a grandson follow in twenty-two years, each one shorter-lived and worse. Nebuchadnezzar carries off the vessels, the people mock the prophets, the temple burns, and the land keeps its Sabbaths for seventy years, as Jeremiah said.
readings: Verse by verse the chapter is 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:21 in Greek, with two lines added (1:21–22) and many small changes: names, numbers, the warning given to Jeremiah instead of Pharaoh, archers turned into officers. Read this way, it is one of the oldest witnesses to how Jews read Chronicles.
Read as the opening of a book

Read as a book of its own, the chapter sets out what the rest restores. Everything taken here comes back: the temple vessels (2:9–14), the Passover kept again by the returned exiles (7:10–15), the law read in Jerusalem (9:37–55). The book begins with a king's Passover and ends with a scribe's reading of the law.

views.O: In the Greek Old Testament, as Swete prints it, 1 Esdras stands just before Ezra–Nehemiah, so an Orthodox reader meets this chapter as a second telling of the end of Chronicles. Its picture of Josiah, upright before the Lord yet unable to turn back the judgment, reads as a lesson in repentance that comes too late for a nation, though not for a king.
views.H: The events can be dated: Josiah's Passover about 622 BC, his death at Megiddo in 609, the first capture of Jerusalem in 597 and the burning of the temple in 586. The chapter adds no new historical facts to Kings and Chronicles, and several of its changes are mistakes or confusions (Jeconiah for Jehoahaz, 1:32; the son named Jehoiakim, 1:41; the deposed king brought 'up out of Egypt,' 1:36). Its value for historians is as a witness to the Greek and Hebrew text of Chronicles.
views.J: Josephus tells Josiah's death at length: Neco is going to fight the Medes and Babylonians, Josiah blocks him at 'Mendes', and Josephus blames fate; he says Jeremiah's elegy for Josiah still existed in his day (Antiquities 10.74–78). The Talmud asks why so good a king died in battle and answers, through Rabbi Yohanan, that he did not consult Jeremiah (Taanit 22b), close to what 1 Esdras 1:26 says outright.
views.S: Of the 55 verses, 2 have no parallel (1:21–22), about 12 say the same as Chronicles, and the rest differ in some detail. The largest changes: the gifts of 1:7; 'morning' for 'cattle' (1:10); Zechariah and Eddinus for Heman and Jeduthun (1:14); Jeremiah's words for Neco's (1:26); officers for archers (1:27); Josiah climbing into his chariot himself (1:29); the names of Josiah's sons (1:32, 1:41); no relation given for Zedekiah (1:44); 'the King of their ancestors' (1:48); 'the LORD's chests' (1:51). See the notes on each verse.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant readers met this chapter in the Latin Vulgate's appendix, as 3 Esdras, or in the Apocrypha of older English Bibles such as the KJV. Neither counts it as Scripture. Scholars in both traditions use it to check the Greek and Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 35–36, and the notes on those chapters on this site cite it.

deep.h: Why a book about the return starts with Josiah
deep.b:
1 Esdras could have begun with Cyrus, as Ezra does. Instead it begins two generations earlier, with Josiah's Passover, and the choice shapes the whole book. Josiah's Passover is the last great feast of the first temple; the returned exiles' Passover is the first great feast of the second (7:10–15, parallel Ezra 6:19–22). Josiah tears down; Ezra rebuilds. The vessels Nebuchadnezzar takes in this chapter are counted out and sent home in the next.

The two added verses (1:21–22) explain why the fall came even after a good king: the sins of the people were already written down, and the words of the Lord had "risen up" against them. That is the same answer 2 Kings gives (2 Kings 23:26–27). Read this way, chapter 1 is the reason for everything after it: Jerusalem fell for its sins, and was given back because the Lord kept his word through Jeremiah (1:55; 2:1).

Three ancient tellings of Josiah's death answer the question of why he died in different ways. 2 Kings gives no reason (2 Kings 23:29). Chronicles says he "did not listen to Neco's words from God's mouth" (2 Chronicles 35:22): God spoke through the enemy king, and Josiah did not hear. 1 Esdras says he did not heed "the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord" (1:26). The Talmud has Rabbi Yohanan say that Josiah should have asked Jeremiah, and Rav that Neco's 'God who is with me' was his idol (Taanit 22b). Josephus blames fate (Antiquities 10.76).

Each answer guards something: Chronicles guards God's freedom to speak through anyone; 1 Esdras and the rabbis guard the idea that God speaks to Israel through his prophets; Josephus writes for Greek and Roman readers who knew the language of fate. The text of 1 Esdras does not say whether its writer found 'Jeremiah' in his Hebrew copy or put the name there himself.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:21; 2 Kings 23:21–25:21; Exodus 12:1–20; Leviticus 26:34–35; Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; Lamentations 4:20; Zechariah 12:11; Daniel 1:1–2; Daniel 9:2; Ezekiel 17:11–21

settings.to: The Levites of the Jerusalem temple
settings.when: Before the Passover in Josiah's eighteenth year (about 622 BC)
settings.why: To set the Levites to their new work: with the ark at rest in the temple, they no longer carry it, so they are to serve the Lord and the people by slaughtering and preparing the Passover in order, by David's arrangements and Moses' command.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of the last centuries BC who already knew Chronicles and Ezra; where and when the book was made is debated (see the book's opening pages). The earliest reader we can watch is Josephus, writing in Rome in the AD 90s, who follows 1 Esdras's wording and order in Antiquities 10–11.

settings.by: The king of Egypt (Neco II, not named here)
settings.to: King Josiah, as he marches to block the Egyptian army
settings.when: 609 BC, as Pharaoh goes north to the Euphrates
settings.why: To turn Josiah aside: Pharaoh claims the Lord sent him to the Euphrates, not against Judah. In 1 Esdras the reader is told in the next verse that the real warning Josiah ignored came through Jeremiah, so Pharaoh's words become a test the king fails.

title: The Decree and the Letter
sum: Seventy years pass between two verses. In the first year of Cyrus, the Lord rouses the Persian king to keep Jeremiah's word, and he sends a proclamation through his empire: the Lord of Israel, the Lord Most High, has made him king of the whole world and told him to build a house in Jerusalem. Heads of families, priests and Levites set out, helped by their neighbors. Cyrus hands the temple vessels to his treasurer, who hands them to Sanassar, and they go home to Jerusalem: 5,469 pieces, by a count that adds up.

Then, in the book's own order, comes trouble. Under Artaxerxes, officials in Samaria write to the king that the Jews are rebuilding a rebel city, its walls and a temple, and that if it is finished he will lose his provinces. The king searches the records, agrees, and orders a halt. The officials ride to Jerusalem with horsemen and stop the work, and the temple stands unfinished until the second year of Darius. The next chapter opens at Darius's court.
readings: Read straight through, the chapter puts Artaxerxes between Cyrus and Darius, which does not match the order of the Persian kings. Josephus noticed and changed the king to Cambyses (Antiquities 11.21). Read this way, the chapter is a historical puzzle.
Read as the setup for chapters 3–4

Read as story, the halt is needed: it leaves the temple unbuilt, so that a young guard at Darius's court can win the king's leave to finish it (4:42–57). Ezra's aside about later opposition becomes the problem that the book's own court tale solves.

views.O: Orthodox readers who have 1 Esdras in their Bible read this chapter beside Ezra 1 and 4, as two tellings of the same return. The decree's opening, that the Lord made a pagan king ruler of the world for the sake of his people, fits the Orthodox reading of God working through earthly rulers in history.
views.H: Historians accept that Cyrus allowed exiles to go home and restore their temples, and that work in Jerusalem was slow until the reign of Darius I (520–515 BC). The Artaxerxes letter belongs, on most reckonings, to the reign of Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC), and concerns the city walls, as in Ezra 4. 1 Esdras's placing of it before Darius, and its adding the temple, are usually taken as the work of the book's writer. 'Coele-Syria and Phoenicia' for 'Beyond the River' is a Greek-period name.
views.J: Josephus follows 1 Esdras here, not the Hebrew Ezra: his Cyrus is king of 'the habitable earth,' his vessel-keeper is Sanabassar, his letter-writers are Rathumus, Beeltethmus and Semellius, and his letter speaks of the temple and of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. He only changes the king's name, to Cambyses, and adds that Cyrus had read Isaiah's prophecy about him (Antiquities 11.1–30).
views.S: All 25 verses have a parallel: 2:1–14 in Ezra 1 and 2:15–25 in Ezra 4:7–24. Only 2:1–2 say the same thing. The main differences: the titles of God in the decree (2:3, 2:5); horses among the gifts (2:6, 2:8); a list of vessels whose numbers add up (2:12–13); a title read as a name (Beeltethmus, 2:15); the temple added to the letter (2:17–18, 2:25); 'Coele-Syria and Phoenicia' for 'Beyond the River'; no 'until I give the order' (2:24). Above all, the letter comes before Darius instead of after him.
views.W: Western readers have used this chapter mostly for its text: the list of vessels and the forms of the officials' names are compared with Ezra 1 and 4 in commentaries on Ezra. Neither the Catholic Church nor Protestant churches count 1 Esdras as Scripture.

deep.b:
Ezra 4 is built like a sermon on opposition, not a timeline. It starts with enemies who hinder the temple "all the days of Cyrus... until the reign of Darius" (Ezra 4:5), then jumps ahead to complaints under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes about the city walls (Ezra 4:6–23), and then goes back: "Then the work on God's house in Jerusalem stopped" until Darius (Ezra 4:24). Many readers take 4:6–23 as an aside, gathering later troubles into one place.

1 Esdras reads the passage as a sequence. It moves the Artaxerxes letter to just after Cyrus's decree, adds the temple to the officials' complaint (2:17–18), and makes the king's reply the reason the temple work stopped (2:25). The cost is chronology: Artaxerxes now reigns before Darius. Whether 1 Esdras misread Ezra, reworked it on purpose to make room for the story of the three guards, or kept an older arrangement of the material is one of the main questions about the book; see the book's opening pages. Josephus solved the problem in his own way by calling the king Cambyses (Antiquities 11.21).

echoes: Ezra 1:1–11; Ezra 4:7–24; 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1; Jeremiah 29:10; Haggai 1:1; Nehemiah 2:1–8; Daniel 5:2–4

settings.to: The Jews in his empire, and the people living around them, by proclamation and in writing
settings.when: In the first year of his reign over Babylon (538 BC)
settings.why: To give the exiles leave to go up and build the house of the Lord of Israel in Jerusalem, and to order their neighbors to help with gold, silver, gifts, horses and livestock. For the book's readers, the pagan king's words prove Jeremiah right: the Lord, not Cyrus, ended the exile.

settings.by: Rathymus the recorder, Samellius the scribe and their council, officials living in Samaria and the province
settings.when: Placed by 1 Esdras before the reign of Darius; in Ezra 4 it belongs to the reign of Artaxerxes I
settings.why: To persuade the king that a rebuilt Jerusalem would refuse tribute and cost him his western provinces, and so to stop the building. In 1 Esdras the complaint includes the temple, so the letter becomes the cause of the long halt.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews of the last centuries BC who already knew Chronicles and Ezra; where and when the book was made is debated (see the book's opening pages). views: 1 Esdras sets the letter between Cyrus and Darius and makes it about the temple too.
In Ezra the letter concerns the city walls in the later reign of Artaxerxes I, and is gathered into Ezra 4 as an example of opposition.

settings.to: Rathymus, Beeltethmus, Samellius and their colleagues in Samaria, Syria and Phoenicia
settings.why: To order the building stopped after a search of the records found that Jerusalem had a past of revolt and of strong kings who ruled the region. Unlike Ezra 4:21, the order leaves no room for a later change ('until I give the order').
